subject: Mathematics
title: Arjun's Kitchen: Rational Expressions and Algebraic Fractions
hook: Arjun mixes recipes and splits bills. Learn how fractions hide inside algebra.

slides.title: Fractions in Disguise
slides.storyContext: Arjun's restaurant needs to scale recipes, split bills, and manage ingredient ratios. He discovers that algebra and fractions work together—algebraic fractions appear everywhere.

image.alt: Fractions in Disguise — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: The Recipe Scaling Problem
slides.storyContext: A recipe needs (x/2) liters of milk for (x + 1) people. Aman asks: "If the recipe is halved, how much milk per person?" Arjun realizes: the answer is a fraction of a fraction—an algebraic fraction: (x/2) ÷ (x + 1) = x / (2(x + 1)).

image.alt: The Recipe Scaling Problem — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Finding the Pattern
slides.storyContext: Neha tracks the cost per serving. For x servings, the total cost is (5x + 20) rupees. The cost per serving is (5x + 20)/x. She notices: when x doubles, the cost per serving barely changes. Arjun says: "Let me simplify that fraction."

points.text: Cost per serving = (5x + 20)/x = 5 + 20/x.
As x grows large, the 20/x term shrinks, approaching pure 5 rupees per serving.

slides.title: Algebraic Fractions: Fractions with Variables

points.label: Definition
points.text: An algebraic fraction is a fraction where the numerator and/or denominator contain variables (letters). Examples: x/5, 3/(x + 1), (x + 2)/(2x - 1).

points.label: Key rule
points.text: The denominator can NEVER be zero. If x/(x - 3), then x ≠ 3 (because 3 - 3 = 0).

example.problem: In the fraction (2x + 3)/(x - 5), what value of x is NOT allowed?
example.solution: x ≠ 5, because when x = 5, the denominator becomes 5 - 5 = 0, and division by zero is undefined.

slides.inSimpleWords: Algebraic fractions are just fractions, but they use letters. Always remember: the denominator cannot be zero.

image.alt: Algebraic Fractions: Fractions with Variables — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: The Ingredient Ratio
slides.storyContext: Aman asks Arjun: "Your pasta sauce uses (3x + 6) grams of tomatoes and (x + 2) grams of basil. The ratio is (3x + 6)/(x + 2). Can this be simplified?" Arjun pulls out a notepad and factors.

points.text: (3x + 6) = 3(x + 2), so the fraction becomes 3(x + 2)/(x + 2) = 3 (for x ≠ −2).
This means: no matter the batch size, the ratio of tomato to basil is always 3:1.

slides.title: Simplifying Algebraic Fractions

points.label: Method
points.text: Factor the numerator and denominator. Cancel common factors. What remains is the simplified fraction.

example.problem: Simplify (4x + 8) / (2x + 4).

slides.inSimpleWords: To simplify: factor both the top and bottom, then cancel any common factors.

image.alt: Simplifying Algebraic Fractions — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Kitchen Math: Simplifying the Spice Mix
slides.storyContext: Arjun's biryani spice blend uses (2x² + 6x) grams of spices and (x + 3) grams of salt. What is the ratio simplified?

example.problem: Simplify (2x² + 6x) / (x + 3).
example.solution: Factor numerator: (2x² + 6x) = 2x(x + 3). So (2x(x + 3)) / (x + 3) = 2x (for x ≠ −3).

slides.inSimpleWords: Factor out common terms to simplify fractions with polynomials.

slides.title: Multiplying Algebraic Fractions

points.label: Rule
points.text: (a/b) × (c/d) = (ac) / (bd). Multiply tops and multiply bottoms.

points.label: Simplify first
points.text: Before multiplying, cancel common factors across the fractions. This saves work.

example.problem: Multiply (3x / 4) × (2 / x).

slides.inSimpleWords: Multiply fractions by multiplying the tops together and the bottoms together. Then simplify.

image.alt: Multiplying Algebraic Fractions — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Doubling the Batch
slides.storyContext: Arjun needs to make double his usual batch. His recipe fraction for ingredient cost is (x)/(x + 5) rupees per serving. He wants to multiply: (x/(x + 5)) × 2. What's the new cost?

points.text: (x/(x + 5)) × (2/1) = (2x)/(x + 5) rupees per serving.
Notice: the fraction stays in the same form, just the numerator scales.

slides.title: Dividing Algebraic Fractions

points.label: Rule
points.text: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c). Flip the second fraction, then multiply.

slides.inSimpleWords: To divide fractions: flip the second fraction and multiply.

image.alt: Dividing Algebraic Fractions — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Sharing the Profit
slides.storyContext: Arjun's profit is (4x + 8) rupees. He divides it equally among (x + 2) partners. But he made a mistake—he divided by (1/(x + 2)) instead. How does this flip change the answer?

example.problem: Simplify (4x + 8) ÷ (1/(x + 2)).
example.solution: (4x + 8) × (x + 2) / 1 = (4x + 8)(x + 2) = 4(x + 2)(x + 2) = 4(x + 2)². This shows flipping magnifies—dividing by a fraction is multiplication by its reciprocal.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividing by a small fraction gives a large result. Flip and multiply to make this clear.

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Algebraic Fractions

points.label: Same denominator
points.text: (a/c) + (b/c) = (a + b) / c. Just add the numerators.

points.label: Different denominators
points.text: Find a common denominator, convert each fraction, then add. Example: 1/x + 1/2 = 2/(2x) + x/(2x) = (2 + x) / (2x).

slides.inSimpleWords: To add/subtract: get the same denominator, combine the numerators, then simplify.

image.alt: Adding and Subtracting Algebraic Fractions — Fractions in Disguise

slides.title: Calculating Total Cost
slides.storyContext: Arjun's fixed cost per day is 1000/(x + 10) rupees (where x is servings). His variable cost is 50/x rupees per serving. Neha asks: "What is the total cost per serving combined?" Arjun needs to add two fractions with different denominators.

points.text: Common denominator: x(x + 10).

slides.title: Arjun's Real Problem
slides.storyContext: Arjun's restaurant budget is split: (2x + 5) rupees for ingredients, (x - 1) rupees for labor. The total cost per meal is 1 / [(2x + 5) / (x - 1)] rupees. Simplify this.

example.problem: Simplify 1 / [(2x + 5) / (x - 1)].

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its flip.

slides.title: Checking the Work
slides.storyContext: Aman solved a problem and simplified (x² - 4)/(x - 2). He got x + 2. But he didn't check for restrictions. Arjun says: "Wait—what if x = 2?" Let's see what happens.

points.text: At x = 2: numerator = 0, denominator = 0 → undefined (indeterminate form).
Always state the restriction: x ≠ 2.

slides.title: Restrictions in Algebraic Fractions

points.label: What are restrictions?
points.text: Values of the variable that make the denominator zero and are forbidden.

points.label: How to find them
points.text: Set denominator = 0 and solve. These x-values are excluded from the domain.

example.problem: List all restrictions for (x + 5) / [(x - 1)(x + 3)].
example.solution: Set denominator = 0: (x - 1)(x + 3) = 0. So x = 1 or x = −3. Restrictions: x ≠ 1, x ≠ −3.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always identify which values of x make the denominator zero and forbid them.

slides.title: The Mistake
slides.storyContext: Aman tries to simplify (x + 5)/(x + 2) by canceling the x's in numerator and denominator. Arjun stops him: "No! You can only cancel factors, not terms." Aman realizes his error and learns to factor first.

points.text: WRONG: (x + 5)/(x + 2) ≠ 5/2. You cannot cancel individual terms.
CORRECT: Factor completely first, then cancel common factors.

slides.title: Common Mistakes to Avoid

points.label: Mistake 1
points.text: Canceling terms instead of factors. (x + 5)/(x + 2) cannot be simplified—there are no common factors.

points.label: Mistake 2
points.text: Forgetting restrictions. Always list forbidden values of x.

points.label: Mistake 3
points.text: Dividing by fractions incorrectly. Always flip the second fraction, then multiply.

example.problem: Is (x + 3)/(x + 3) = 1 always true?
example.solution: Yes, for x ≠ −3. At x = −3, both numerator and denominator are 0—indeterminate. Always state restrictions.

slides.inSimpleWords: Factor before canceling. Watch out for zero denominators. Flip fractions when dividing.

slides.title: The Bill Mess-Up
slides.storyContext: Neha calculates the cost per person for a bill of (4x + 12) rupees split among (x + 3) people. Arjun factors and simplifies to get 4 rupees per person. But wait—what if x = -3?

points.text: The restriction x ≠ −3 means no negative people—it makes sense in context too.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Bill Split
slides.storyContext: Three friends split a restaurant bill of (3x² + 6x) rupees equally among (x + 2) people. How much per person?

example.problem: Simplify (3x² + 6x) / (x + 2).
example.solution: Factor: 3x(x + 2) / (x + 2) = 3x (after canceling (x + 2)).

slides.inSimpleWords: Factor the numerator, cancel common terms with the denominator, and simplify.

slides.title: Challenge: Complex Fraction
slides.storyContext: Aman encounters a 'complex fraction'—a fraction within a fraction. He needs to simplify: [1/(x + 1)] / [1/(x + 2)].
slides.inSimpleWords: A fraction divided by a fraction? Flip the bottom and multiply.

slides.title: Aman Multiplies Correctly
slides.storyContext: Aman practices: (x² + 4x)/(x + 2) × (x + 2)/(x). He factors first, cancels, then multiplies. Arjun approves: "Good—simplify before multiplying, not after. It saves confusion."

points.text: Cancel before multiplying: x and (x + 2) cancel, leaving (x + 4).

slides.title: Challenge: Three Operations Combined
slides.storyContext: Arjun combines multiply and subtract: (x + 2)/(x) × (x²)/(x + 2) - 1.

example.problem: Simplify (x + 2)/(x) × (x²)/(x + 2) - 1.
example.solution: Multiply: [(x + 2) × x²] / [x × (x + 2)] = x² / x = x (for x ≠ 0, −2). Subtract: x - 1.

slides.inSimpleWords: Combine operations step by step. Multiply first, then simplify, then subtract.

slides.title: Aman's Insight
slides.storyContext: Aman realizes: "Every recipe, every cost calculation, every work problem boils down to fractions. Algebraic fractions let us solve them all with one set of rules—variables just make them general."

points.text: Algebraic fractions = the language of relationships between quantities.
Once you master the rules, you can solve any problem about proportions, costs, or mixtures.

slides.title: Neha's Final Question
slides.storyContext: At day's end, Neha asks: "Why do we even study algebraic fractions? When will I use this?" Arjun smiles: "Every time you calculate costs per person, ratios, rates, or anything that scales. They're the language of change."

points.text: Algebraic fractions model real situations: cost per unit, work rates, concentration formulas.
They connect arithmetic to algebra—a bridge between numbers and variables.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Algebraic fractions have variables in numerator or denominator. The denominator can never be zero.
Simplify by factoring and canceling common factors.
Multiply: (a/b) × (c/d) = (ac)/(bd). Divide: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c).
Add/subtract: find a common denominator first, then combine.
Always identify restrictions: values that make the denominator zero are forbidden.

slides.inSimpleWords: Algebraic fractions work like regular fractions—use the same rules, but with variables. Always watch for restrictions.

image.alt: What We Learned — Fractions in Disguise

subject: Mathematics
title: Pradeep's Field: The Right Triangle Mystery
hook: An ancient Indian mathematician and a Greek one both discovered the same truth about right triangles. Pradeep finds it in his farm.

slides.title: The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem
slides.storyContext: Pradeep's square field must be divided by a diagonal fence into two right triangles. How long is the diagonal? Shastri tells him of an ancient formula discovered in India over 2000 years ago.

image.alt: The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: The Ancient Discovery
slides.storyContext: Shastri explains: "Over 2,000 years ago, Baudhayana, an Indian mathematician and priest, wrote the Sulbasutras. He discovered that for right-angled figures, the diagonal of a square equals the sides combined in a special way."

points.text: This knowledge was used to build altars and temples with perfect right angles.
Later, the Greeks discovered the same truth. Pythagoras lived centuries after Baudhayana.

slides.title: Measuring the Diagonal
slides.storyContext: Pradeep has a square plot 12 meters × 12 meters. He wants to fence diagonally. To calculate the fence length, Shastri says: "In ancient India, Baudhayana wrote: in a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of squares of the other two sides." Pradeep realizes this solves his problem.

image.alt: Measuring the Diagonal — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: The Three Parts of a Right Triangle
slides.storyContext: Anjali draws a right triangle. She labels: the two sides meeting at the right angle (legs) and the longest side across from it (hypotenuse). Pradeep asks: "Which measurements go in the Baudhayana formula?"

points.text: Legs: the two sides touching the right angle (90° corner).
Hypotenuse: the longest side, always opposite the right angle.
The formula relates these three: hypotenuse² = leg1² + leg2².

slides.title: The Theorem: a² + b² = c²

points.label: Statement
points.text: In a right triangle, if the two legs (shorter sides) are a and b, and the hypotenuse (longest side, opposite the right angle) is c, then: a² + b² = c².

points.label: Which side is which?
points.text: The hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle (90° angle). The legs meet at the right angle.

example.problem: In a right triangle with legs 3 and 4, what is the hypotenuse?

slides.inSimpleWords: In any right triangle, if you square the two shorter sides and add them, you get the square of the longest side.

image.alt: The Theorem: a² + b² = c² — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: The Pattern of Squares
slides.storyContext: Anjali draws three squares: one on each leg and one on the hypotenuse. She asks: "What if the area of the leg squares equals the area of the hypotenuse square?" Shastri nods: "That is exactly the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem, shown visually."

points.text: Area of square on leg a = a².
Area of square on leg b = b².
Area of square on hypotenuse c = c² = a² + b².

slides.title: Finding the Hypotenuse

points.label: Given legs a and b
points.text: Use c² = a² + b², then take the square root: c = √(a² + b²).

example.problem: A ladder leans against a wall. The base is 6 meters from the wall, the wall is 8 meters tall. How long is the ladder?
example.solution: This forms a right triangle with legs 6 and 8. Ladder = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find the hypotenuse: square both legs, add them, then take the square root.

image.alt: Finding the Hypotenuse — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Pradeep's First Calculation
slides.storyContext: Pradeep measures his 12 × 12 meter square field and calculates the diagonal using the theorem.

example.problem: Find the diagonal of a 12 × 12 meter square.
example.solution: Diagonal² = 12² + 12² = 144 + 144 = 288. Diagonal = √288 = 12√2 ≈ 16.97 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: For a square with side a, the diagonal is a√2.

slides.title: Finding a Missing Leg

points.label: If you know c and a, find b
points.text: Rearrange: b² = c² - a², so b = √(c² - a²).

points.label: Example
points.text: Hypotenuse 13, one leg 5: other leg = √(169 - 25) = √144 = 12.

example.problem: A right triangle has hypotenuse 15 and one leg 9. Find the other leg.

slides.inSimpleWords: To find a missing leg: square the hypotenuse, subtract the square of the other leg, then take the square root.

image.alt: Finding a Missing Leg — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Anjali's Discovery
slides.storyContext: Anjali experiments with different leg lengths: 3 and 4, then 5 and 12, then 8 and 15. Each time, the hypotenuse comes out to a whole number. She tells Shastri: "These are special!"

slides.title: Pythagorean Triples: Special Whole-Number Triangles

points.label: Definition
points.text: A Pythagorean triple is a set of three whole numbers a, b, c where a² + b² = c². All three sides are integers—no square roots needed.

example.problem: Is (6, 8, 10) a Pythagorean triple?
example.solution: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10². Yes, it is a Pythagorean triple (and it is 2 × (3, 4, 5)).

slides.inSimpleWords: Pythagorean triples are right triangles where all three sides are whole numbers. They are very useful for quick calculations.

image.alt: Pythagorean Triples: Special Whole-Number Triangles — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Quick Calculation with Triples
slides.storyContext: Pradeep's friend has a 5-meter ladder leaning against a wall. If the base is 3 meters from the wall, how high up the wall does it reach?

example.problem: Ladder length 5 m, distance from wall 3 m. Find height on wall.
example.solution: This is the 3-4-5 triple. Height² = 5² - 3² = 25 - 9 = 16. Height = 4 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: Recognizing Pythagorean triples saves calculation time—no need for square roots.

slides.title: Proving a Right Triangle: Converse of the Theorem

points.label: Converse
points.text: If a² + b² = c² is true, then the triangle is a right triangle. You can use this to check if a triangle is right-angled.

points.label: Example
points.text: Sides 5, 12, 13: check 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13². Yes, it is right-angled.

example.problem: Is a triangle with sides 7, 24, 25 right-angled?
example.solution: Check: 7² + 24² = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25². Yes, it is right-angled.

slides.inSimpleWords: If two sides squared and added equal the third side squared, then that triangle has a right angle.

image.alt: Proving a Right Triangle: Converse of the Theorem — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Testing a Field
slides.storyContext: A surveyor claims Anjali's rectangular field has right angles. Shastri suggests: "Measure the corners. If two sides are 30 and 40 meters, the diagonal should be 50 meters if it is truly right-angled."

points.text: If 30² + 40² = 50², then the corner is a right angle.
900 + 1600 = 2500. ✓ Yes, the corner is right-angled.

slides.title: Pradeep's Diagonal
slides.storyContext: Pradeep's square field is 12 meters × 12 meters. The diagonal creates two right triangles with legs 12 and 12.

example.problem: Find the diagonal length of a 12 × 12 meter square field.
example.solution: Diagonal² = 12² + 12² = 144 + 144 = 288. Diagonal = √288 = 12√2 ≈ 16.97 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: The diagonal of a square with side a is a√2.

image.alt: Pradeep's Diagonal — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: The Temple Corner
slides.storyContext: Shastri tells the story: "Ancient temple builders used the 3-4-5 triangle to ensure perfect right angles. They tied a rope with 12 knots: 3 units, 4 units, 5 units—a perfect right triangle every time."

points.text: The 3-4-5 triple was known in India long before Pythagoras in Greece.
Builders used this for construction and altar-building with perfect accuracy.

slides.title: Checking Anjali's Measurement
slides.storyContext: Anjali measures a corner of a room using a tape measure: one wall is 3.6 meters, the other is 4.8 meters, and the diagonal is 6 meters. Is this corner exactly 90°?

points.text: And 6² = 36.0. Yes, exactly 90°!

slides.title: The Converse in Practice: Verifying Right Angles

points.label: Application
points.text: When building, surveying, or measuring, use the converse to verify. If a² + b² = c², the angle is definitely 90°.

points.label: Real example
points.text: Carpenters build square frames by checking: if sides are 6 ft and 8 ft, the diagonal must be 10 ft. If it's not, the frame is not square.

example.problem: A carpenter wants a square frame 5 × 5. What should the diagonal be?
example.solution: Diagonal² = 5² + 5² = 50. Diagonal = √50 ≈ 7.07 feet. If the measured diagonal differs, the frame is not square.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the theorem to verify corners are truly 90°. Measure two sides and the diagonal, then check the equation.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Village Path
slides.storyContext: A village path goes 9 meters east, then 12 meters north. What is the straight-line distance from start to end?

example.problem: Find the straight-line distance when traveling 9 meters east and 12 meters north.
example.solution: This forms a right triangle with legs 9 and 12. Distance = √(9² + 12²) = √(81 + 144) = √225 = 15 meters.

slides.inSimpleWords: When two perpendicular paths form a right angle, the direct distance is found using the Pythagorean theorem.

image.alt: Your Turn: The Village Path — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

slides.title: Challenge: Is It Right-Angled?
slides.storyContext: Three surveyors report different measurements for a field's sides: 20, 21, and 29 meters. Is this field right-angled?

example.problem: Check if sides 20, 21, 29 form a right triangle.
example.solution: Assume 29 is the longest (hypotenuse). Check: 20² + 21² = 400 + 441 = 841. And 29² = 841. Yes, it is right-angled! (20, 21, 29) is a Pythagorean triple.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use the converse to verify: if the squares of two sides sum to the square of the longest side, it is right-angled.

slides.title: Shastri's Timeline
slides.storyContext: Shastri explains the history: "Baudhayana lived around 800 BCE. Pythagoras lived around 570 BCE—over 200 years later! Yet they discovered the same truth independently." Anjali realizes: "Great minds see the same patterns."

points.text: Baudhayana: Sulbasutras (Indian, ~800 BCE).
Pythagoras: Greek (~570 BCE), got the fame but came later.

slides.title: Why Squares Matter

points.label: The geometry
points.text: The theorem describes areas. a² is the area of a square with side a. The visual proof: three squares fit together perfectly in a right triangle.

points.label: The algebra
points.text: c² = a² + b² is the mathematical statement of that visual fact.

example.problem: A right triangle has legs 6 and 8. What are the areas of the three squares?
example.solution: Square 1 (leg 6): area = 36. Square 2 (leg 8): area = 64. Square 3 (hypotenuse): area = 36 + 64 = 100, so hypotenuse = 10.

slides.inSimpleWords: The three squares on the three sides of a right triangle have areas that satisfy a² + b² = c².

slides.title: Challenge: Finding Hidden Hypotenuses
slides.storyContext: Three right triangles with legs: (5, 12), (8, 15), (7, 24). Find all hypotenuses without a calculator, using Pythagorean triples.

example.problem: Find c for (5, 12), (8, 15), (7, 24) using Pythagorean triple knowledge.
example.solution: (5, 12) → 13 (multiply (3,4,5) by different factors or recognize it). (8, 15) → 17 (recognize (8,15,17) triple). (7, 24) → 25 (recognize (7,24,25) triple). All are known triples!

slides.inSimpleWords: Memorize common Pythagorean triples to solve quickly without square roots.

slides.title: Anjali's Pride
slides.storyContext: Anjali reflects: "Baudhayana discovered this 2,300 years ago, without calculators or computers. Just geometry and observation. And it still works perfectly today." Shastri smiles: "Mathematics is eternal."

points.text: The Pythagorean theorem is one of humanity's oldest, most universal truths.
It works in architecture, navigation, physics, engineering—everywhere.

slides.title: Pradeep's Final Check
slides.storyContext: Before building his fence, Pradeep double-checks: the diagonal of his 12 × 12 field should be 12√2 meters, about 16.97 meters. He measures with a long rope—yes, it fits exactly. The ancient knowledge holds.

points.text: Theory: 12² + 12² = 288, so diagonal = √288 = 12√2.
Practice: the rope measurement confirms it. Theory and reality agree.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: The Pythagorean theorem: a² + b² = c² for any right triangle.
The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.
Find the hypotenuse: c = √(a² + b²). Find a leg: a = √(c² - b²).
Pythagorean triples are whole-number right triangles like (3, 4, 5).
Check if a triangle is right-angled using the converse: if a² + b² = c², it is right-angled.
This ancient Indian knowledge, discovered by Baudhayana, is fundamental to geometry and engineering.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Pythagorean theorem connects the sides of any right triangle. Master the two steps: square, add (or subtract), then root.

image.alt: What We Learned — The Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem

subject: Mathematics
title: Meera's Recipe and Ratios: Direct and Inverse Proportion
hook: Meera discovers that some quantities always stay in balance—when one doubles, so does the other. But some work the opposite way.

slides.title: Proportional Reasoning-2
slides.storyContext: Meera scales recipes for her bakery. When she doubles the flour, the cookies double. But when more workers arrive, the work gets done faster. Grandma explains: two different kinds of proportion.

image.alt: Proportional Reasoning-2 — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: The Two Mysteries
slides.storyContext: Meera notices: her cookie recipe needs 2 cups of flour for 24 cookies. Dev asks: "What about 48 cookies?" Meera doubles the flour. Then Grandma adds a twist: "If 2 workers frost 24 cookies in 1 hour, how long for 1 worker?" Dev pauses. Grandma smiles: "That is different—inverse proportion."

points.text: Flour doubles → cookies double (direct proportion).
Workers halve → time doubles (inverse proportion).

slides.title: The Cookie Mystery
slides.storyContext: Meera's cookie recipe needs 2 cups of flour for 24 cookies. Dev asks: "How much flour for 48 cookies?" Meera: "Double the flour, double the cookies—4 cups!" Then Grandma says: "But here's the twist: if 2 workers frost 24 cookies in 1 hour, how long for 1 worker?" Dev hesitates. Grandma smiles: "That is inverse proportion."

image.alt: The Cookie Mystery — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Grandma's Explanation
slides.storyContext: Grandma draws two scenarios: "In direct proportion, both go up together—like flour and cookies. In inverse proportion, one goes up and the other goes down—like workers and time. It's like a seesaw!"

points.text: Direct: same direction. Inverse: opposite directions.
Direct uses division to find the constant. Inverse uses multiplication.

slides.title: Direct Proportion: Both Increase Together

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two quantities are directly proportional if when one increases, the other increases by the same factor. If one doubles, so does the other. If one halves, so does the other.

points.label: Formula
points.text: If y is directly proportional to x, then y = kx, where k is the constant of proportionality.

example.problem: A recipe needs 3 eggs for 12 cookies. How many eggs for 36 cookies?
example.solution: Cookies tripled (12 → 36), so eggs triple: 3 → 9 eggs. Or using y = kx: k = 3/12 = 1/4, so for 36 cookies: eggs = (1/4) × 36 = 9.

slides.inSimpleWords: In direct proportion, when one thing grows, the other grows in the same way. Double one, double the other.

image.alt: Direct Proportion: Both Increase Together — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Flour and Cookies
slides.storyContext: Meera's master recipe: 2 cups flour makes 24 cookies. What if she wants to make 12, 24, 48, or 72 cookies?

example.problem: Complete: 2 cups → 24 cookies. 1 cup → ? 4 cups → ? 6 cups → ?
example.solution: Direct proportion: halve flour (1 cup) → 12 cookies. Double flour (4 cups) → 48 cookies. Triple flour (6 cups) → 72 cookies. Constant k = 12 cookies/cup.

slides.inSimpleWords: The ratio of flour to cookies stays constant. k = cookies / flour = 24/2 = 12.

slides.title: Finding the Constant of Proportionality

points.label: Method
points.text: If y = kx, then k = y/x. Divide corresponding values to find k.

points.label: Check consistency
points.text: Calculate k for multiple pairs. If k is always the same, the quantities are directly proportional.

example.problem: Does this data show direct proportion? (cost Rs 10 for 5 items, Rs 20 for 10 items, Rs 30 for 15 items)
example.solution: k = 10/5 = 2, k = 20/10 = 2, k = 30/15 = 2. Yes, k is constant at 2. The equation is cost = 2 × items.

slides.inSimpleWords: To check if quantities are directly proportional: divide one by the other for each pair. If the ratio is always the same, they are directly proportional.

image.alt: Finding the Constant of Proportionality — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: The Frosting Dilemma
slides.storyContext: Meera watches her team frost cookies. 4 workers frost all the cookies in 2 hours. She asks: "If I had only 2 workers, how long would it take?" Grandma explains: "Fewer workers means more time for the same job. That's inverse proportion."

points.text: 4 workers × 2 hours = 8 worker-hours of work (constant).
2 workers × ? hours = 8 worker-hours. ? = 4 hours.

slides.title: Inverse Proportion: One Increases, the Other Decreases

points.label: Definition
points.text: Two quantities are inversely proportional if when one increases, the other decreases by the same factor. If one doubles, the other halves.

points.label: Formula
points.text: If y is inversely proportional to x, then y = k/x, or xy = k, where k is the constant of proportionality.

example.problem: 2 workers frost 24 cookies in 1 hour. How long would 1 worker take?
example.solution: Fewer workers → more time. Workers halved (2 → 1), so time doubles (1 → 2 hours). Using xy = k: 2 × 1 = 2, and 1 × 2 = 2. Both give k = 2.

slides.inSimpleWords: In inverse proportion, when one thing doubles, the other halves. They multiply to a constant.

image.alt: Inverse Proportion: One Increases, the Other Decreases — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Frosting Rate Chart
slides.storyContext: Meera makes a chart: how many hours to frost 240 cookies with different numbers of workers?

example.problem: 1 worker takes 8 hours. 2 workers? 4 workers? 8 workers?
example.solution: Constant k = workers × hours = 1 × 8 = 8. For 2 workers: 2 × hours = 8, so 4 hours. For 4: 2 hours. For 8: 1 hour. Each doubling of workers halves the time.

slides.inSimpleWords: As workers multiply, time divides. The product stays the same.

slides.title: Speed, Time, and Distance: A Classic Inverse Case

points.label: Formula
points.text: Distance = Speed × Time, or Time = Distance / Speed. If distance is fixed and speed doubles, time halves.

points.label: Example
points.text: To travel 120 km: at 40 km/h takes 3 hours; at 60 km/h takes 2 hours; at 80 km/h takes 1.5 hours.

example.problem: A 300 km trip takes 5 hours at one speed. How long at double the speed?
example.solution: Original: Time = 300/60 = 5 hours (speed = 60 km/h). Double speed: 120 km/h. New time = 300/120 = 2.5 hours (halved).

slides.inSimpleWords: Speed and time are inversely proportional for a fixed distance. Double the speed, half the time.

image.alt: Speed, Time, and Distance: A Classic Inverse Case — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Dev's Road Trip
slides.storyContext: Dev drives 240 km to his aunt's house. At 60 km/h, it takes 4 hours. He realizes: if he drove at 80 km/h, it would only take 3 hours. He asks: "Is speed and time inversely proportional?" Grandma nods and shows the math.

points.text: Time = Distance / Speed = 240 / 60 = 4 hours.
Speed × Time = constant. 60 × 4 = 240 (the distance).

slides.title: Recognizing and Checking Inverse Proportion

points.label: Method
points.text: Multiply corresponding x and y values. If the product is always the same (constant k), the quantities are inversely proportional.

points.label: Example
points.text: Workers and time to finish: (2 workers, 3 hours), (3 workers, 2 hours), (6 workers, 1 hour). Check: 2×3=6, 3×2=6, 6×1=6. All equal, so inversely proportional.

example.problem: Is this inverse proportion? (pressure 2 atm, volume 60L), (3 atm, 40L), (4 atm, 30L)
example.solution: Check products: 2×60=120, 3×40=120, 4×30=120. All equal, so yes, inversely proportional. k = 120.

slides.inSimpleWords: To check inverse proportion: multiply corresponding values. If the product is always the same, they are inversely proportional.

image.alt: Recognizing and Checking Inverse Proportion — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Picking Orders
slides.storyContext: Grandma receives berry-picking orders. She assigns workers: 1 worker can pick 100 kg in 10 hours. 2 workers can pick 100 kg in 5 hours. She notices: the total work (worker-hours) stays constant at 10. This is inverse proportion at work.

points.text: 1 worker × 10 hours = 10 worker-hours = 100 kg of berries.
2 workers × 5 hours = 10 worker-hours = 100 kg of berries.
More workers mean less time, but the total work is the same.

slides.title: Meera's Bakery Scaling
slides.storyContext: Meera receives orders for 1, 2, and 3 batches of cookies. Direct proportion: flour amounts scale. But workers and time scale inversely.

example.problem: Meera's recipe (1 batch): 2 cups flour, 4 workers frost 12 cookies/hour. For 3 batches, how much flour and how many hours for 1 worker to frost?
example.solution: Flour (direct): 2 × 3 = 6 cups. Frosting rate: 4 workers frost 12 cookies/hour means 1 worker frosts 3 cookies/hour. For 36 cookies (3 batches): time = 36/3 = 12 hours.

slides.inSimpleWords: Ingredients scale directly with batch size. Time scales inversely with number of workers.

image.alt: Meera's Bakery Scaling — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: The Grocery Shop Deal
slides.storyContext: Dev buys apples: 1 kg costs Rs 80, 2 kg costs Rs 160, 3 kg costs Rs 240. He checks: is this direct proportion? Yes—double the kg, double the cost. Constant k = 80 rupees/kg.

points.text: Formula: cost = 80 × kg. This is direct proportion.

slides.title: The Project Teams
slides.storyContext: Grandma runs a sewing project. 1 person takes 24 days to complete a dress order. 2 people take 12 days. 4 people take 6 days. She notices: multiply people by days, always get 24.

points.text: Constant: people × days = 24 (total work). This is inverse proportion.

slides.title: Writing Equations for Proportions

points.label: Direct: y = kx
points.text: If you know one pair of values, find k = y/x, then write the full equation.

points.label: Inverse: xy = k or y = k/x
points.text: If you know one pair, find k = x × y, then write the equation.

example.problem: At 60 km/h, a trip takes 4 hours. Write the direct relationship between speed and distance (fixed trip).
example.solution: Distance = constant. Distance = speed × time. 240 = 60 × 4. For any speed s: time t = 240/s (inverse relationship). Or: s × t = 240.

slides.inSimpleWords: Direct: divide to find k (y/x). Inverse: multiply to find k (x×y). Then write the equation.

slides.title: Meera's Pricing
slides.storyContext: Meera sets a bakery price: cupcakes cost Rs 40 each. She makes a table: 1 → Rs 40, 5 → Rs 200, 10 → Rs 400. Is this direct? Yes.

example.problem: Write the direct proportion equation: cost = ? × cupcakes.
example.solution: k = cost / cupcakes = 40 / 1 = 40. Equation: cost = 40 × cupcakes.

slides.inSimpleWords: From one data point, find k, then predict any other value.

slides.title: The Pool Filling
slides.storyContext: Grandma fills a pool. 1 hose takes 20 hours. 2 hoses take 10 hours. But 4 hoses might not take 5 hours—why? Because real-world limits (pressure drop, hose interference) break the ideal inverse proportion.

points.text: Ideal inverse: 1 × 20 = 2 × 10 = constant.
Reality: real systems have friction, limits, and delays that break pure math.

slides.title: Proportions in the Real World

points.label: When proportions work
points.text: Shopping (price per item), recipes (ingredients scale), speed-time (fixed distance), workers on simple tasks.

points.label: When they break down
points.text: Real systems have limits: too many workers can interfere, pressure drops with more hoses, diminishing returns exist.

example.problem: A bakery makes 100 cakes/day with 5 bakers. Does doubling to 10 bakers make 200 cakes?
example.solution: Maybe not—they might get in each other's way, share ovens, or hit equipment limits. Theory says yes (inverse: time ÷ 2). Reality: maybe 180 cakes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Proportions model simple systems perfectly. Real systems are more complex.

slides.title: Your Turn: The Water Tank Problem
slides.storyContext: A water tank fills at different rates. 2 pumps fill it in 6 hours. How long with 3 pumps?

example.problem: 2 pumps fill a tank in 6 hours. How long with 3 pumps?
example.solution: Pumps and time are inversely proportional. More pumps → faster filling. 2 × 6 = 12 (constant). With 3 pumps: 3 × time = 12, so time = 4 hours.

slides.inSimpleWords: When more pumps work together, the job finishes faster. This is inverse proportion.

image.alt: Your Turn: The Water Tank Problem — Proportional Reasoning-2

slides.title: Challenge: Mixed Scenarios
slides.storyContext: Meera gets four data sets. Which show direct proportion, which show inverse, and which show neither?

example.problem: Direct or inverse? (1) Flour doubles → cookies double. (2) Workers triple → time becomes one-third. (3) Eggs double → cost doubles. (4) Price per kg increases → kilos bought decreases.
example.solution: (1) Direct: y = 12x. (2) Inverse: xy = constant. (3) Direct: y = kx. (4) Inverse: xy = constant (total budget). All four have clear relationships.

slides.inSimpleWords: Identify patterns: same direction = direct. Opposite direction = inverse.

slides.title: Meera Predicts Sales
slides.storyContext: Meera notices: when she lowers cupcake price from Rs 50 to Rs 40, she sells more. At Rs 50, she sells 200/day. At Rs 40, she sells 250/day. Is this inverse?

points.text: Lower price → more sales. The product (revenue per budget-conscious customer) is constant.

slides.title: Recognizing Proportions in Tables

points.label: Direct proportion table
points.text: Ratios y/x are constant. Each x increase brings the same y increase per unit.

points.label: Inverse proportion table
points.text: Products x × y are constant. A change in one is exactly offset by the opposite change in the other.

slides.inSimpleWords: Check the table: divide for direct (same ratio), multiply for inverse (same product).

slides.title: Grandma's Caution
slides.storyContext: Grandma tells a cautionary tale: "A shop once doubled its workers thinking output would double (direct). But they got tangled up, and output only went up 50%. Real systems aren't always proportional!"

points.text: Math assumes ideal conditions.
Reality has complexity: interference, diminishing returns, physical limits.

slides.title: Challenge: Finding k from Tables
slides.storyContext: Dev has data but doesn't know if it's direct or inverse. Table: (x=2, y=15), (x=3, y=10), (x=5, y=6).

example.problem: Is this direct or inverse? Find k. (2,15), (3,10), (5,6)
example.solution: Try direct: k = y/x = 15/2=7.5, 10/3≈3.33, 6/5=1.2 (not constant, not direct). Try inverse: k = x×y = 2×15=30, 3×10=30, 5×6=30 (constant! inverse). Equation: xy = 30, or y = 30/x.

slides.inSimpleWords: Always test both: divide for direct, multiply for inverse. See which gives a constant k.

slides.title: Meera's Bakery Success
slides.storyContext: Meera reflects: "Now I understand why doubling ingredients doubles cookies (direct), but more workers don't always cut time in half (inverse reality). Proportions are the pattern—but reality is messier."

points.text: Understanding proportions gives a foundation for making predictions.
Real systems then add complexity on top of this base.

slides.title: What We Learned

points.text: Direct proportion: y = kx. When one increases, so does the other by the same factor. Check by dividing: y/x = k (constant).
Inverse proportion: y = k/x or xy = k. When one increases, the other decreases. Check by multiplying: x × y = k (constant).
Recipes and ingredients: direct. Workers and time: inverse.
Speed and time (fixed distance): inverse. Distance and cost at fixed rate: direct.
Always check: divide for direct, multiply for inverse. See if the result is constant.

slides.inSimpleWords: Two quantities either grow together (direct) or grow in opposite directions (inverse). Check by dividing (direct) or multiplying (inverse).
